about: The Codex: every word Prism uses, in plain English. One file, shared by every G4 program and by Ted. Claude draft 2026-10-17 — Sailor's to edit.
intro: I'm Ted. This is the Codex — every word Prism uses, in plain English. Tap a word to look it up, or ask me anything.

object.text: The actual thing the news is about — a law, an order, a court ruling, a deal, a seat in Congress. Prism keeps the object in view so the conversation can't drift off it onto personalities or vibes.

reading.text: One object, and what people are saying about it, laid out so you can place yourself. You read the story, set how hard you'd argue, pick the answer closest to yours, and pin it on the map.

sides.text: Prism sorts voices into four corners: left or right, and establishment or populist. Establishment voices speak from inside institutions — agencies, big papers, party leaders. Populist voices speak against them. The corner says where a voice comes from, not whether it's right.

dial.text: How hard you'd push your view in an argument. The middle (fluid) is just saying what you think. Further out (coalition) is trying to win people over. The far ends (denominated) are making the point even if it costs you friends.

z.text: Your read on what actually happened to the object. Up means it did what it promised; down means it didn't. It's separate from whether you like it.

graphmap.text: The square you place yourself on. Left and right run across; establishment is the top half and populist the bottom. Height above or below the square is z. Drag to turn it.

pin.text: Where you stand on a reading. Tap the map to place it, drag to move it, set z, then commit. Pins stay on your phone unless you sign in to post them.

field.text: Everyone's pins on the same reading, so you can see where you landed compared with other people.

legislators.text: How close a member of Congress stands to your pins, from +100 (right beside you) to −100 (the far side). It uses their voting record, or their own words on a reading when we have them.

parallelogram.text: One published segment or article — a show, a column, a news piece — cut down to the lines about the object and scored. Parallelogram (capital P) is the publication that collects them.

heat.text: How heated the words are, 0 to 100. Low is plain statement; high is all-out argument.

says.text: What a segment says happened to the object — for example, whether the deal will help or won't. Mixed means it went both ways.

clarity.text: How much of a segment sticks to the facts of the object, 0 to 100. It's worked out from the other scores, not a judgement of the show.

floor.text: A daily baseline from Bloomberg's The Close — the business press's own reading — that other segments can be compared against. It's one point of view, not neutral ground.

burns.text: The strip of stories the newsroom is watching. Each frame says where that story stands: watching, has a reading, you pinned it, gone quiet, or turned around.

sst.text: The needle on BloomBurger's front page: the share of the world's traded energy that's paid for in dollars, month by month. Falling means less of it is sold in dollars.

bloomburger.text: Prism's news desk: everything Prism collects from the media, and the Parallelogram feed built from it.

dreamgetty.text: The 3D villa Prism lives in. The columns, the Venus de Milo and Ted come from there, and the G4 sits inside it.

g4.text: The computer Prism runs on — in the villa, it's an old iMac G4. On your phone, you're looking at its screen.

ted.text: Ted Turner, a coyote. He shows people around the villa and answers questions here.
